choices.text: A substance that accepts an electron pair
A substance that donates an electron pair
choices.why: That is a Lewis base.

choices.text: A substance that donates a proton
choices.why: That is the Brønsted–Lowry definition. Proton donors are Lewis acids too, but the Lewis definition is broader.

choices.text: A substance that accepts a proton
choices.why: That is a Brønsted–Lowry base.

explanation: A Lewis acid is a substance that accepts an electron pair, and a Lewis base is a substance that donates an electron pair. The donated pair is shared between the acid and the base in a covalent bond.

choices.text: A substance that donates an electron pair
A substance that accepts an electron pair
choices.why: That is a Lewis acid.

choices.text: A substance that donates H^+
choices.why: Donating H^+ makes a substance an acid, not a base.

choices.text: A substance with a vacant, low-energy orbital
choices.why: A vacant orbital lets a substance accept an electron pair, which makes it a Lewis acid.

explanation: A Lewis base is a substance that donates an electron pair: a compound with a pair of nonbonding electrons that it can use to bond to a Lewis acid.

prompt: Why is the Lewis definition of acids and bases more encompassing than the Brønsted–Lowry definition?

choices.text: It isn't limited to substances that donate or accept protons
It applies only to reactions in water
choices.why: Being limited to water would make it narrower, not broader. It is broader because it covers electron-pair acceptors that have no proton, such as BF3.

choices.text: It counts only substances that contain hydrogen
choices.why: The opposite: Lewis acids such as Mg^2+, BF3, and AlCl3 have no hydrogen at all.

choices.text: It treats acids as electron-pair donors
choices.why: Lewis acids accept electron pairs; Lewis bases donate them.

explanation: The Lewis definition is more encompassing because it's not limited to substances that donate or accept just protons. Any electron-pair acceptor is a Lewis acid, which includes many species besides H^+.

prompt: In a Lewis acid–base reaction, what happens to the electron pair donated by the base?

choices.text: It is shared between the acid and the base in a covalent bond
It is transferred completely, forming an ionic bond
choices.why: The pair isn't handed over; it becomes a shared, covalent bond between the base and the acid.

choices.text: It stays as a lone pair on the base
choices.why: The base uses that lone pair to bond to the acid, so it is no longer nonbonding.

choices.text: It is released as two separate electrons
choices.why: The electrons move as a pair, into a vacant orbital on the acid, forming a bond.

explanation: The donated electron pair is shared between the acid and the base in a covalent bond: the base's filled orbital and the acid's vacant orbital combine to give the product B–A.

prompt: To accept an electron pair, what must a Lewis acid have?

choices.text: Either a vacant, low-energy orbital or a polar bond to hydrogen so it can donate H^+
A lone pair of nonbonding electrons
choices.why: A lone pair is what a Lewis base needs, so it can donate an electron pair.

choices.text: A negative charge
choices.why: Many Lewis acids are neutral (BF3) or positive (Mg^2+); what matters is room to accept a pair.

choices.text: A filled valence shell
choices.why: With a filled shell there is nowhere to put an incoming pair; Lewis acids such as BF3 have unfilled valence orbitals.

explanation: A Lewis acid must have either a vacant, low-energy orbital or a polar bond to hydrogen so that it can donate H^+, which has an empty 1s orbital.

prompt: Why is the metal cation Mg^2+ a Lewis acid?

choices.text: It accepts a pair of electrons when it forms a bond to a base
It donates H^+
choices.why: Mg^2+ has no hydrogen to donate. It is an acid only in the Lewis sense, as an electron-pair acceptor.

choices.text: It donates a pair of electrons to a base
choices.why: Donating an electron pair is what a Lewis base does.

choices.text: Metal cations are Lewis bases, not acids
choices.why: Metal cations such as Mg^2+ accept electron pairs, which makes them Lewis acids.

explanation: Various metal cations, such as Mg^2+, are Lewis acids because they accept a pair of electrons when they form a bond to a base. Certain metabolic reactions begin with an acid–base reaction between Mg^2+ and an organic diphosphate or triphosphate ion as the Lewis base.

prompt: Why are group 3A compounds such as BF3 and AlCl3 Lewis acids?

choices.text: They have unfilled valence orbitals that can accept electron pairs
They have lone pairs they can donate
choices.why: Donating a lone pair would make them Lewis bases. Boron and aluminum have room for more electrons, not extra pairs.

choices.text: They release H^+ in water
choices.why: BF3 and AlCl3 contain no hydrogen; they are acids only in the Lewis sense.

choices.text: They are metal cations
choices.why: They are neutral compounds. Their acidity comes from the unfilled valence orbital on the group 3A atom.

explanation: Compounds of group 3A elements, such as BF3 and AlCl3, are Lewis acids because they have unfilled valence orbitals and can accept electron pairs from Lewis bases (Figure 2.11.1).

prompt: Which of these is a Lewis acid even though it has no hydrogen to donate?

choices.text: FeCl3
CH3NH2 (methylamine)
choices.why: Methylamine's nitrogen has a lone pair it can donate, so it acts as a Lewis base.

choices.text: CH3OCH3 (dimethyl ether)
choices.why: Dimethyl ether is the Lewis base in Figure 2.11.1: it donates a lone pair from oxygen to BF3.

choices.text: H2O
choices.why: Water has hydrogens it can donate as H^+, and it also acts as a Lewis base with its two lone pairs.

explanation: Many transition-metal compounds, such as TiCl4, FeCl3, ZnCl2, and SnCl4, are Lewis acids. Like BF3 and AlCl3, they accept electron pairs without having any H^+ to donate.

prompt: In the reaction of boron trifluoride with dimethyl ether (Figure 2.11.1), which statement is correct?

choices.text: Dimethyl ether is the Lewis base, donating a lone pair from oxygen to a vacant orbital on boron
BF3 is the Lewis base, donating a lone pair from fluorine
choices.why: BF3 is the Lewis acid: its boron has a vacant valence orbital that accepts the pair.

choices.text: Dimethyl ether is the Lewis acid, accepting electrons from boron
choices.why: The ether's oxygen has nonbonding electrons to give; electrons flow from the ether to BF3.

choices.text: BF3 donates H^+ to the ether
choices.why: BF3 has no hydrogen. The reaction forms a B–O bond from the oxygen's lone pair.

explanation: Dimethyl ether, the Lewis base, donates an electron pair to a vacant valence orbital of the boron atom in BF3, a Lewis acid, forming an acid–base complex.

prompt: In a Lewis acid–base reaction, which way does the curved arrow point?

choices.text: From the electron pair on the base to the acid
From the acid to the base
choices.why: Curved arrows follow the electrons, and the electrons move from the base, which donates them, to the acid.

choices.text: From the H^+ to the base
choices.why: Arrows show electron movement, not the movement of the proton; they start at the base's lone pair.

choices.text: Either way, since the arrow only links acid and base
choices.why: The direction matters: it shows the flow of the electron pair from base to acid.

explanation: The direction of electron-pair flow from base to acid is shown using a curved arrow, just as curved arrows showed electron flow between resonance structures in Section 2.5.

prompt: In the electrostatic potential maps of Figure 2.11.1, how do boron and oxygen change when BF3 reacts with dimethyl ether?

choices.text: Boron becomes more negative and oxygen more positive
Boron becomes more positive and oxygen more negative
choices.why: That is backward: boron gains electrons from the oxygen's lone pair, and oxygen gives them up.

choices.text: Both become more negative
choices.why: The electrons move from oxygen to boron, so oxygen loses electron density while boron gains it.

choices.text: Neither changes
choices.why: Electrons flow from the base to the acid, so the charge on both atoms changes.

explanation: In the electrostatic potential maps, the boron becomes more negative (red) after reaction because it has gained electrons, and the oxygen atom becomes more positive (blue) because it has donated electrons.

prompt: When H2O reacts with HCl to form H3O^+, how does water act as a Lewis base?

choices.text: It donates one of oxygen's nonbonding electron pairs to an H^+
It donates an H^+ to the chloride
choices.why: Donating H^+ would make water an acid. Here HCl is the acid and water accepts the H^+.

choices.text: It accepts an electron pair from HCl
choices.why: Accepting an electron pair is what a Lewis acid does.

choices.text: It uses a vacant orbital on oxygen
choices.why: Oxygen in water has a filled octet with two lone pairs; it gives one of those pairs.

explanation: H2O, with its two pairs of nonbonding electrons on oxygen, acts as a Lewis base by donating an electron pair to an H^+ in forming the hydronium ion, H3O^+.

prompt: How many lone pairs of electrons does the oxygen of a divalent oxygen compound, such as an alcohol or ether, have?
explanation: A divalent oxygen compound has two lone pairs of electrons, which is why most oxygen-containing organic compounds can act as Lewis bases.

prompt: How many lone pairs of electrons does the nitrogen of a trivalent nitrogen compound, such as an amine, have?
explanation: A trivalent nitrogen compound has one lone pair of electrons, which it can donate as a Lewis base.

prompt: When acetaldehyde, CH3CHO, acts as a Lewis base toward an acid HA, which atom donates the electron pair?

choices.text: The oxygen atom
The C=O carbon
choices.why: That carbon uses all four valence electrons in bonds and has no lone pair to donate.

choices.text: The hydrogen on the C=O carbon
choices.why: Hydrogen has no lone pairs. The base site is the atom with nonbonding electrons.

choices.text: The CH3 carbon
choices.why: The CH3 carbon has four bonds and no lone pair; only the oxygen has nonbonding electrons.

explanation: A Lewis base donates an electron pair, so we locate the lone pairs on acetaldehyde: they are on the oxygen. A curved arrow from an oxygen lone pair to the H of HA shows the electron flow (Worked Example 2.11.1).

prompt: Alcohols and carboxylic acids can act as both acids and bases. When do they act as bases?

choices.text: When their oxygen atom accepts an H^+
When they donate an H^+
choices.why: Donating an H^+ is how they act as acids.

choices.text: When their carbon atom accepts an electron pair
choices.why: Accepting an electron pair would be Lewis acid behavior; as bases they use an oxygen lone pair.

choices.text: Never; only nitrogen compounds act as bases
choices.why: Most oxygen-containing organic compounds can act as Lewis bases because oxygen has lone pairs.

explanation: Some compounds can act as both acids and bases, just as water can. Alcohols and carboxylic acids act as acids when they donate an H^+, but as bases when their oxygen atom accepts an H^+.

prompt: When acetic acid is protonated by sulfuric acid, where does the H^+ add, and why?

choices.text: On the doubly bonded oxygen, because that product is stabilized by two resonance forms
On the singly bonded oxygen, because that oxygen already carries a hydrogen
choices.why: That product is not formed; protonation on the singly bonded oxygen gives a less stable ion.

choices.text: On both oxygens at once
choices.why: In such cases the reaction normally occurs only once, giving the more stable product.

choices.text: On the CH3 carbon
choices.why: A base site needs a lone pair; in acetic acid only the oxygens have them.

explanation: Acetic acid could be protonated on either oxygen. The reaction normally occurs only once, and the more stable product forms: protonation occurs on the doubly bonded oxygen because that product is stabilized by two resonance forms.
